quote_item10: We found that 1.1% of tweets from Twitter contained misinformation on COVID-19, with 5 (0.7%) of 746 tweets after discarding non-English posts in batch 1 and 6 (2.8%) of 211 tweets after discarding non-English posts in batch 2, compared to 0.3% on Weibo, with 1 (0.4%) of 279 posts in batch 1 and 1 (0.2%) of 441 posts in batch 2
notes: Kreps, George, Watson, Cai & Ding, JMIR Infodemiology 2022. Content analysis of 3,579,575 COVID-keyword posts (2,344,322 tweets, 1,235,243 Weibo posts) from two 24-hour windows, 30-31 January and 6-7 February 2020; a 1% random sample of each keyword stream, then a random 5-7% of that sample hand-coded (957 English tweets, 720 Weibo posts). Item1/2 HIGH: the universe is a keyword-seeded topical corpus ('coronavirus', 'covid-19' and their Chinese equivalents), not an audience; the Weibo arm comes from the third-party Weibo-COV crawl whose coverage of the platform is never established, and the Twitter arm was pulled through an academic API registered in December 2020, i.e. ten months after the posting window, so any tweet deleted or suspended in between is silently absent from a frame used to count misinformation. Item3 LOW: selection is random at both stages, a 1% random sample of the keyword stream (15,737/1,572,928; 7,726/771,404; 4,914/491,353; 7,439/743,890) and then a random number 0-100 with a cut at 5 for manual coding (954, 448, 279, 441). Items4/5 NA: content-only design, no respondents and no person-level trace. Item6 LOW under the instrument: accuracy calls are adjudicated against the WHO Mythbusters fact-check page, an external and pre-existing standard, which is what item 6 asks for. FLAGGED, NOT OVERRIDDEN: the 11 tweets printed in Textbox 1 show the WHO page was not what actually drove the coding. Several coded items are commentary ABOUT misinformation rather than false claims ('deeply ridiculous: indian government slammed for recommending homeopathy for coronavirus prevention ... what is the harm of tolerating pseudoscience? sigh'; a tweet saying bioweapon conspiracy theories reminded the poster of a 2011 film), one is a news report ('sf officials urge public to attend lunar new year celebration'), and one ('cave full of bats in china identified as source of virus almost identical to the one killing hundreds today') tracks the contemporaneous scientific account. Only the camel-urine cure maps onto a Mythbusters entry. The instrument asks whether an external standard exists, not whether it was applied well, so item 6 stays LOW and the failure of application is carried by item 7. Item7 HIGH: three coders, an independent first pass, a team recode and a lead-coder deconfliction, but no kappa, no alpha and no agreement rate of any kind; the topic categories borrow Fung et al., the accuracy judgement uses no validated instrument at all. Item8 HIGH: the two arms reach the coders by different routes, Twitter scraped directly through the academic API and Weibo taken from the Weibo-COV secondary corpus, and non-English posts were discarded from the Twitter samples (954 to 746, and 448 to 211, a 53% trim in batch 2) with no matching trim on the Weibo side, yet the headline 'almost 4 times' ratio is read off the two rates without adjustment. Item9 HIGH: two 24-hour windows generalised to prevalence, and the second straddles the death of Li Wenliang, which the paper itself reports as the top trending Twitter keyword of batch 2; the authors concede the results 'are not generalizable'. Item10 LOW: within each arm numerator and denominator are a matched pair, misinformation posts over all posts coded in that arm (11/957 and 2/720), randomly drawn from the analysed total and not selected on the outcome; the topical curation of the frame is penalised at items 1-2 and is not counted a second time here. Small print: Methods give 2,344,332 tweets and Results 2,344,322, a 10-post discrepancy; both rates rest on single-digit numerators (11 and 2), which is a precision problem and deliberately not a Hoy bias item.
